transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-02-18 15:00 UTC
Duration: 75m
Attendees: Ethan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Jonas (Redwood Infra), Aisha (Redwood Solutions), Dr. Michael Tan (Zenith ML), Jane Park (CTO), Samir (Cloud Arch), Lina (Product)

Summary:
Quick technical deep-dive on supporting extremely long contexts (>=128k tokens) for clinical record stitching and multi-document prompts. Discussed KV cache strategies, chunking/overlap heuristics, attention optimizations (FlashAttention / grouped attention), quantization tradeoffs for long-sequence memory, and VPC/on-prem constraints for Zenith's regulatory environment. Decided to run a 128k benchmark on Dedicated + VPC with sample dataset and report back.

Topics covered:
- long-context architecture patterns
- memory/kv-cache management and eviction policies
- chunking strategies and overlap stitching
- batching and latency tradeoffs at 128k sequences
- quantization (4-bit vs 8-bit) effects on memory + perf
- VPC/on-prem deployment networking, KMS and audit logs

Transcript:
[00:00] Ethan: hey everyone, thanks for making time, this is the deep technical session we scoped after the discovery. i'll kick off and then priya will go into the runtime diagrams.
[00:32] Jane Park: thanks, quick note — our core use-case is stitching a patient's entire longitudinal record plus external docs, that's why 128k+ context is a hard requirement. latency under 2s per 1k tokens would be ideal for background batch but we also need some interactive sub-second parts for triage workflows.
[01:10] Priya: got it. we'll walk through high-level approaches: sliding-window chunking with overlap, external KV-indexing where we only load relevant kv-slices, and segmented attention (mixing local attention for recent tokens and cached global summaries).
[01:45] Dr. Michael Tan: when you say "kv-slices" what exactly gets in memory? we've seen blowups when the sequence length growth is linear, we can't just keep 128k tokens in GPU memory for many concurrent requests.
[02:10] Jonas: yeah straight to the point — naive transformer will allocate O(seq^2) attention buffers, that's impossible. our runtime uses optimized attention kernels (FlashAttention++ variant) and dynamic kernel selection to avoid the full seq^2 in many paths. we also do prefix kv caching so repeated prefixes don't get recomputed.
[02:50] Samir: prefix cache is great but we operate inside a VPC with strict egress, also HSM/KMS for key material. how does caching work across nodes? replication or sharded?
[03:20] Priya: two modes: sharded KV cache pinned to GPU nodes for lowest latency (requires stateful routing), or a cold-store + on-demand fetch (S3-like) for memory-constrained clusters. for Zenith we recommended sharded + safe eviction policy with a persistent index so replays are consistent.
[04:05] Lina: what about chunk boundaries and hallucinations? stitching docs across chunks is tricky.
[04:28] Priya: agreed. our approach is overlap + anchor tokens plus a short rerank pass. chunking heuristic: 8k chunks with 512 token overlap for clinical notes, but for 128k we do hierarchical summarization — we compute local chunk embeddings, store summaries in cache, then a second-pass attend-to-summaries before hitting raw tokens. reduces attention cost significantly.
[05:10] Dr. Michael Tan: hierarchical summarization sounds promising but accuracy concerns — we can't abstract away critical datapoints. can you control recall vs cost?
[05:45] Ethan: yes, that's where quantization & pruning choices come in plus the routing policy — hot segments (recent events, flagged clinical keywords) stay fully materialized in cache; cold history is summarized. customers can pin ranges to be retained verbatim.
[06:20] Jane Park: about quantization — we've tried static 4-bit and saw some regression on entity extraction. what's Redwood's recommendation for long context?
[06:45] Priya: short answer — prefer mixed precision: 8-bit for attention/key/value storage, 4-bit for weights where we can accept small degradation. for long context, kv memory precision matters: storing kv in 8-bit or float16 keeps retrieval fidelity higher. we recommend 4-bit quant for MLP/weights when unit cost pressure is high, plus calibration runs.
[07:15] Jonas: also, we have experimental quantization-aware KV packing that uses 6-bit effective storage but decodes to 8-bit for compute, it's a tradeoff and we can run benchmarks.
[07:40] Samir: how about CPU offload? our on-prem nodes are limited GPU RAM but have beefy host memory. can the runtime spill to host and still meet latency targets?
[08:05] Priya: yes, spilling to host is supported. it increases latency for the spilled ranges by ~2-4x, depending on PCIe gen and NVMe configs. for interactive low-latency paths we keep hot segments on GPU, spill cold ranges. for batch/async pipelines we can accept higher latency and save cost.
[08:40] Dr. Michael Tan: numbers? can you give ballpark tokens/sec for 128k single stream?
[09:00] Jonas: ballpark — a single A100-like node with optimized kernels and kv-sharding can do ~1500-3000 decode tokens/sec on long-context workloads when most of the heavy history is summarized. If you keep the full 128k materialized in GPU memory for a single stream you'll be limited to low hundreds due to memory and attention cost. Dedicated pools with batching across streams improve throughput, but latency per request varies.
[09:45] Lina: what about batching at 128k? doesn't batching create huge memory multiplication?
[10:02] Priya: yes. batching long sequences increases peak memory multiplicatively. we do continuous batching: micro-batches that share prefix computations using the KV cache, and we prioritize batching of similar length sequences. for Zenith use-case we suggested a hybrid: background batch jobs for full-record scoring, interactive single-request optimized paths for triage.
[10:40] Jane Park: are there optimizations to attention itself — like sparse attention or grouped query attention?
[11:02] Jonas: we support grouped attention (segmented attention where nearby tokens attend densely and distant tokens use low-rank or sampled attention). we also have support for sparse patterns for certain architectures. FlashAttention vs varients: FlashAttention reduces memory during compute but you still need kv storage; grouped attention avoids quadratic blowup for long-range by approximating global context.
[11:45] Dr. Michael Tan: curious about correctness with approximate attention — we need to run QA on critical sequences.
[12:10] Priya: absolutely. we pair approximate paths with evaluation harnesses — regression tests, targeted prompt suites, and metrics that track recall of entity spans. you can gate automatic fallbacks on metric thresholds — if the approximate attention path drops below a recall spec, fallback to full attention for that request.
[12:40] Samir: VPC questions — do you require outbound egress for model updates or metrics? we need to keep everything inside our network for compliance.
[12:58] Ethan: for Redwood Private we can run the control plane in customer VPC or use a local control-plane option. model binaries can be pushed over secure channels; you can lock down egress and we can ship an air-gapped bundle for on-prem. telemetry can be streamed to your internal endpoints or disabled.
[13:30] Lina: KMS integration? we need HSM-backed keys for PHI workflows.
[13:45] Jonas: we support KMS/HSM integrations (AWS KMS, Azure KeyVault, on-prem HSMs). keys never leave your boundary in Private mode and audit logs are exportable.
[14:10] Priya: quick note on deployment topology: for low-latency triage we prefer a dedicated GPU pool per region with stateful routing and pinned KV shards; for batch backfill we use elastic Dedicated nodes with cold storage attached.
[14:40] Dr. Michael Tan: okay demo request — can you run a POC with our sample 120k clinical threads and show latency + token cost, including 4-bit vs 8-bit configurations?
[15:05] Ethan: yes — priya will run two benchmark matrices: (A) 128k full materialized path (if feasible), (B) hierarchical summarization + kv-shard path. each will include 4-bit/8-bit weight variants and CPU spill configs.
[15:30] Priya: expected deliverables: perf logs, flamegraphs of memory usage, per-step latency breakdown (tokenization, attention, kv fetch), and a recommended config.
[15:50] Samir: timeline? we need to validate before our vendor review on 2026-03-01.
[16:05] Priya: we'll aim to have initial bench results by 2026-02-23 and a POC plan by 2026-02-20.
[16:25] Jane Park: security team will want SOC2 docs and data retention policy.
[16:40] Ethan: sending SOC2 + architecture whitepaper and the VPC checklist in follow-up.
[17:00] Dr. Michael Tan: on batching metrics — can you expose token-level cost and a way to map tokens to patient-record ranges for chargeback?
[17:18] Jonas: yes our console exposes token-level breakdown and route-level cost. we also export logs for traceability with token->request mapping (PII redacted or hashed on request).
[17:40] Lina: edge case: say we pin the first 30k tokens verbatim and summarize the rest. how do you ensure that pinned range stays consistent if we upgrade model versions?
[18:05] Priya: model pinning is supported — you can pin model version + pinned token ranges. we keep a migration tool that verifies pinned ranges post-upgrade and runs regression prompts. if the new model fails validation we auto-fallback to previous variant for those routes.
[18:35] Dr. Michael Tan: any notes on single-stream replication for HA? stateful KV shards are a potential single point.
[19:00] Jonas: we replicate KV indexes across N+1 nodes asynchronously; we can accept slightly higher write latency for higher durability. for failover we rehydrate shards from persistent storage. tradeoff: higher replication increases memory footprint.
[19:28] Ethan: branding note — the runtime references in docs as "Redwood Serving Runtime" sometimes get transcribed as "Redwood Serving Time" in our notes, ignore typos.
[19:45] Jane Park: okay to discuss pricing? we want a model that doesn't explode for background jobs.
[20:02] Ethan: we'll propose Dedicated reserved capacity with burst for POC and a usage-based overlay for background large-batch processing. we'll include unit economics per 1k effective tokens considering chunking and summarization savings.
[20:25] Priya: final technical notes: we also support checkpointed KV snapshots for long-term retention, and fast rehydration using memory-mapped files if you prefer local disk-backed caches in on-prem setups.
[20:50] Samir: can we control eviction policy rules? e.g., pin patient ranges and evict based on access frequency plus clinical priority tags.
[21:08] Priya: yes eviction policies are pluggable: LRU, TTL, priority-based, or customer-specified pin lists.
[21:30] Dr. Michael Tan: do you have guidance for chunk size for clinical text vs scanned documents? OCR noise complicates embedding recall.
[21:50] Priya: scanned docs — larger chunk sizes (12-16k) with tighter overlap and OCR-cleaning pre-pass work better; embedding deduping and fuzzy-match anchors reduce redundant retrievals.
[22:10] Jane Park: any gotchas with long tokenization? utf8 vs clinical char sets?
[22:30] Jonas: tokenizer choices matter — for mixed English + clinical shorthand we pre-tokenize and normalize. subword tokenization can blow up counts if not normalized; we recommend a preprocessing stage to reduce token inflation.
[22:55] Lina: great. recap and next steps?
[23:10] Ethan: recap: Redwood to run 128k perf matrix (Priya + Jonas), deliver by 2026-02-23, provide VPC checklist and SOC2 artifacts (Ethan), Zenith to share sample dataset and infra config (Samir) by 2026-02-20. schedule follow-up POC planning meeting next week.
[23:40] Dr. Michael Tan: thanks all, excited to see the numbers.
[23:50] Ethan: thanks — we'll follow up in email with links to the benchmark tracker and the POC plan.
